stem: A 34-year-old stable on levothyroxine starts a combined estrogen contraceptive. Eight weeks later she is tired and her TSH has risen. She takes her tablet correctly on an empty stomach. What explains this?
correct: Estrogen raises thyroid-binding globulin, so her need rises

distractors.text: Estrogen binds levothyroxine in the gut like calcium
distractors.why: Binding in the gut is calcium, iron and antacids.

distractors.text: Estrogen induces CYP enzymes that clear levothyroxine
distractors.why: The inducers taught are rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine.

distractors.text: Estrogen blocks conversion of T4 to T3 in the tissues
distractors.why: That is PTU, iodine and steroids in storm.

distractors.text: Estrogen causes hyperthyroidism, as amiodarone can
distractors.why: Her TSH is high: she needs more hormone.

why_correct: Estrogens raise thyroid-binding globulin, so levothyroxine needs rise.
takeaway: New estrogen on levothyroxine: expect a higher dose.
discriminator: More binding protein, not less absorption.

stem: A 63-year-old with type 2 diabetes on basal insulin starts prednisone 40 mg daily for a COPD flare. Which plan is most appropriate?

distractors.why: Steroids raise glucose.

distractors.text: Hold insulin; prednisone replaces its metabolic effect
distractors.why: It opposes insulin's effect on glucose.

distractors.text: Add spironolactone to prevent steroid hyperkalemia
distractors.why: Hyperkalemia is not the steroid problem here.

distractors.text: Stop prednisone abruptly at day 5 to protect the axis
distractors.why: Abrupt stops are the risk after long courses, and this is not the issue asked.

takeaway: Steroid course in a diabetic: plan for higher glucose.
discriminator: The steroid changes the insulin need.

stem: A 52-year-old with acromegaly has taken octreotide for a year. IGF-1 is at goal. He now reports episodes of right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals and a resting pulse of 52. Which explanation fits best?

distractors.text: Pegvisomant toxicity: liver injury needing liver tests
distractors.why: He takes octreotide; liver tests are the pegvisomant concern.

distractors.text: Cabergoline effect: orthostatic hypotension and nausea
distractors.why: Those are dopamine-agonist effects, not his drug.

distractors.text: Tumor growth: the pituitary mass is pressing locally
distractors.why: IGF-1 is at goal and the symptoms are biliary.

distractors.text: Desmopressin effect: hyponatremia from retained water
distractors.why: He is not on desmopressin and has no sodium symptoms.

why_correct: Octreotide and lanreotide cause GI upset, gallstones and bradycardia (and glucose changes). Biliary pain plus a slow pulse in a controlled patient is the drug, not the disease.
takeaway: Somatostatin analogs: gallstones, GI upset, bradycardia.
discriminator: Octreotide → gallbladder and pulse; pegvisomant → liver tests.

stem: A 71-year-old started desmopressin for central diabetes insipidus 10 days ago. To 'stay hydrated' he drinks water all day. He is now confused with a headache and nausea. Which step is most appropriate first?

stem: A 39-year-old with Cushing syndrome and type 2 diabetes starts mifepristone. A month later her glucose control is better, but serum cortisol is higher than before. Which interpretation is correct?

distractors.text: Treatment failure: switch to ketoconazole to lower cortisol
distractors.why: Cortisol rises with receptor blockade; levels mislead.

distractors.text: Lab error: cortisol always falls on a receptor blocker
distractors.why: Cortisol levels rise on mifepristone.

distractors.text: Adrenal crisis: give IV hydrocortisone and fluids now
distractors.why: She is improving; nothing suggests crisis.

distractors.text: Expected: also check PSA, which the drug lowers by half
distractors.why: That is the finasteride rule.

stem: A 78-year-old with coronary artery disease and new hypothyroidism (TSH 14 mIU/L) is starting levothyroxine. Which plan is safest?

stem: A 41-year-old with untreated Graves disease arrives with fever 40°C, heart rate 158, agitation and vomiting after an infection. Propranolol has been given. Which sequence is correct for the next drugs?
correct: PTU now, iodine an hour after it, plus hydrocortisone

distractors.text: Iodine now, PTU 1 hour after it, plus hydrocortisone
distractors.why: Iodine before PTU supplies substrate for new hormone.

distractors.text: PTU now, aspirin for the fever, then iodine an hour later
distractors.why: Aspirin frees bound hormone and is avoided in storm.

distractors.text: Methimazole now, with levothyroxine held until afterwards
distractors.why: The storm sequence taught is PTU first, then iodine.

distractors.text: Hydrocortisone alone, since it blocks all hormone release
distractors.why: Steroids help conversion and adrenal cover; they are added.

why_correct: Beta-blocker and PTU come first; iodine is given only after PTU because iodine first would feed new hormone synthesis. Steroids blunt peripheral conversion and cover relative adrenal insufficiency. Aspirin is avoided.
takeaway: Storm order: beta-blocker + PTU, then iodine, plus steroid.
discriminator: PTU blocks synthesis; iodine blocks release, but only after PTU.

stem: A 58-year-old has taken prednisone daily for 8 months for polymyalgia. He ran out 4 days ago. He presents with vomiting, weakness and blood pressure 82/50. What explains this, and what is the treatment?

distractors.text: Steroid excess causing hyperglycemia; give insulin and fluids
distractors.why: He stopped the steroid; this is deficiency.

distractors.text: Mineralocorticoid excess from prednisone; give spironolactone
distractors.why: Spironolactone would worsen hypotension.

distractors.text: Rebound ACTH surge overdriving the adrenal; give ketoconazole
distractors.why: ACTH is suppressed, and the adrenal has shrunk.

why_correct: Chronic steroids suppress CRH and ACTH and the adrenal shrinks. Stopping abruptly leaves the axis unable to make cortisol: adrenal crisis, treated with IV hydrocortisone and fluids. Prevention is a taper.
takeaway: Long steroid course: taper, never stop abruptly.
discriminator: Crisis = too little cortisol after suppression.

stem: A 48-year-old on a stable levothyroxine dose has TSH 9.8 mIU/L. She takes it every morning with breakfast, her calcium carbonate and a new iron tablet. She has not missed a dose. What is the best next step?

distractors.why: Fix absorption first; TSH is rechecked at 6–8 weeks.

discriminator: Absorption problem (binders) vs clearance problem (inducers).
